column2: Seeing him come near in the battle, the wise Vrikodara, mighty, hurled his mace at him with great speed.
Seeing that throw, your son, lord of men, stepped back from the spot, and the mace fell vain on the ground.
Having avoided that blow, your son, in agitation, the best of the Kurus, struck Bhimasena with his mace.
From the blood streaming from him, of immeasurable might, and from the fall of that heavy blow, a faintness seemed to come over him.
Duryodhana knew the Pandava was in distress in the battle, and Bhima steadied his greatly pained body.
He thought him standing ready to strike in the fight, and so your son did not strike him again.
Then, after resting a moment, mighty Bhimasena rushed with speed, O king, at Duryodhana standing there.
Seeing him charging, enraged and of immeasurable might, bull of the Bharatas, wishing to make his blow vain,
your great-minded son, resolving to stand firm, wished to leap up, O king, to cheat Vrikodara.
Bhimasena understood that intent of the king, and rushing at him and leaping aside like a lion,
as he evaded by a feint and was about to leap again, the Pandava hurled his mace at his thighs with speed, O king.
That mace, hurled by the terrible-deeded one, like the crash of a thunderbolt, broke both of Duryodhana's fair thighs.
That tiger among men fell, making the earth resound, his thighs broken by Bhimasena, your son, lord of the earth.
Winds blew with thunder-crashes, dust rained down, and the earth shook with her trees, shrubs and mountains.
When that hero, lord of all kings, fell, a great, loud, blazing, fearful meteor with thunder fell again, as the lord of the earth fell.
Then a rain of blood and a rain of dust fell, Bharata, as Maghavan rained when your son was felled.
A great cry of Yakshas, Rakshasas and Pishachas was heard in the sky, bull of the Bharatas.
At that dreadful sound, a most dreadful sound of beasts and birds arose, of many, on every side.
The horses and elephants that remained there with the men gave out a great cry when your son was felled.
A great sound of kettledrums, conches and mridangas arose, and went even beneath the earth, when your son was felled.
The quarters there, O king, were filled with dreadful headless trunks with many feet and arms, dancing and terrifying.
Banners, missiles and weapons seemed to tremble then, O king, when your son was felled.
Lakes and wells poured out blood, best of kings, and great swift rivers flowed backward.
Women became like men and men like women, O king, when your son Duryodhana fell.
Seeing those wondrous portents, the Panchalas with the Pandavas were all troubled in mind, bull of the Bharatas.
The gods, Gandharvas and Apsarases went as they pleased, telling of the wondrous battle of your two sons, Bharata.
Likewise the perfected, the weather-seers and the Charanas went as they had come, praising the two lions among men.
All the Somakas too, their hair standing on end, saw him like a rutting elephant felled by a lion.
Then mighty Bhimasena, having felled Duryodhana, approached that fallen king of the Kurus and said this:
Formerly, fool, you called Draupadi, in a single garment, 'cow, cow' in the assembly, laughing at us; obtain today the fruit of that derision.
Having said this, he touched the crown of his head with his left foot and rolled the head of the lion among kings with his foot.
Likewise Bhima, red with anger, crusher of strong foes, spoke again, hear what he said, lord of men:

Those who earlier danced before us, saying 'cow, cow' again and again—we dance back at them again, saying 'cow, cow.'
mahabharata:9:58.8	We have no deceit, no fire, no dice, no cheating; relying on the strength of our own arms we crush our enemies.
Having reached the far shore of the enmity, Vrikodara, laughing softly, said to Yudhishthira, Keshava, the Srinjayas, Dhananjaya and the two sons of Madri:
Look at those who brought Draupadi in her season, and those who tore her garment in the assembly: they are slain in battle by the Pandavas through the austerity of Yajnaseni's.
Those cruel sons of King Dhritarashtra who once called us 'sesame-seeds without kernel' are slain with their hosts and kinsmen; whether we go to heaven or hell, as we like.
Again, looking at the fallen king on the ground and that mace on his shoulder, crushing his head with his left foot, he called Duryodhana 'deceiver.'
The righteous-souled best of the Somakas did not approve of that, seeing the foot placed on the king's head by the glad, petty-minded Bhimasena.
Seeing Bhimasena boasting and dancing repeatedly after thus slaying your son, the king of dharma said this:

Do not crush his head with your foot; do not transgress great dharma; he is a king and a kinsman, and he is slain; this is not proper, blameless one.
mahabharata:9:58.16	He is ruined, his ministers slain, his brothers slain, his sons slain, his line of offerings cut off; and this was not done properly by you.
mahabharata:9:58.17	People earlier called you Bhimasena the righteous; why then, Bhimasena, do you stand upon a king?
Seeing Duryodhana so fallen, King Yudhishthira, with eyes full of tears, said these words:

Surely this was ordained by the mighty great-souled Creator, that we should wish to slay you and you us, best of the Kurus.
mahabharata:9:58.20	By your own fault you have met such great calamity, Bharata, from greed, pride and childishness.
mahabharata:9:58.21	Having had your friends, brothers, fathers, sons, grandsons and teachers slain, you have met your end.
mahabharata:9:58.22	Through your fault your mighty brothers and other kinsmen were slain by us; I think fate is hard to overcome.
mahabharata:9:58.23	The daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law of Dhritarashtra, widowed, distraught and wasted with grief, will surely reproach us.
Having said this, the king, greatly afflicted with sorrow, sighed, and Yudhishthira, the son of Dharma, lamented long.
Tell me, Sanjaya, what Rohini's son, skilled and expert in mace-fighting, did.
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing your son struck on the head by Bhimasena, Rama, best of strikers, mighty, was greatly enraged.
Then in the midst of the kings the plough-bearer, raising his arms, uttering a dreadful cry of distress, said, "Fie, fie, Bhima!"

Alas, shame! That a blow was struck below the navel at one of pure valour! Never was such seen in mace-fighting as Vrikodara has done.
mahabharata:9:59.6	'One must not strike below the navel'—that is the settled rule of the scripture; but this fool, ignorant of the scripture, acts as he pleases.
As he spoke thus, great anger arose in him, and the mighty one, raising his plough, rushed at Bhima.
With his arms raised, that great soul's form looked like a great white mountain, variegated with many minerals.
As he sprang forward, Keshava, bowed in humility, though mighty, seized him with his plump, rounded arms with effort.
The white and the dark one, the two best of the Yadus, then shone the more, like the moon and sun in the sky at the day's end, O king.
Keshava said to him, as if calming his rage: "Growth of oneself, growth of friends, growth of friends' friends, and the reverse for foes: these are the six kinds of growth of oneself.
When the reverse comes about for oneself and for friends, let one know the mind's defeat; it should soon bring peace.
The Pandavas, of pure manhood, are our natural friends, our own, sons of our father's sister, grievously wronged by others.
You know that fulfilling a vow is a kshatriya's dharma; Bhima vowed earlier in the assembly hall: 'I shall break Suyodhana's thighs with my mace in a great battle.'
And earlier he was cursed by the great sage Maitreya: 'Bhima will break your thighs with his mace, scorcher of foes.' So I see no fault; do not be angry, slayer of Pralamba.
We are bound to the Pandavas by marriage and by affection; our growth is through their growth; do not be angry, bull among men."
[Rama said:] "Dharma well practised by the good restrains with two others; wealth, for one overly greedy, and desire, for one given to excess.
One who pursues dharma, wealth and desire without harming dharma-and-wealth, dharma-and-desire, or desire-and-wealth enjoys utmost happiness.
All this has been thrown into confusion by Bhimasena's oppression of dharma, Govinda; but as you wish, you speak to me."
[Vasudeva said:] "You are known in the world as free of anger, righteous and ever fond of dharma; therefore be calm, do not be angry.
Know that the Kali age has come, and the Pandava's vow; let the Pandava be quit of the enmity and of his vow."
[Sanjaya said:] Hearing from Keshava even this pretext of dharma, lord of men, Rama, not pleased at heart, spoke in the assembly.

Having slain the righteous Suyodhana unfairly, the Pandava will gain fame in this world as a crooked fighter.
mahabharata:9:59.24	And Duryodhana, righteous, will go to an eternal state; Dhritarashtra's son, the king, slain, was a straight fighter.
mahabharata:9:59.25	Having entered on the vow of battle, spreading the sacrifice of war, offering himself in the fire of his foes, he attained the avabhritha bath of fame.
Having said this, the mighty son of Rohini mounted his chariot, like a peak of white cloud, and set out for Dvaraka.
When Rama had gone to Dvaravati, the Panchalas, the Vrishnis and the Pandavas, lord of men, were not very glad at heart.
Then Vasudeva said this to Yudhishthira, dejected, downcast with thought, his resolve stricken with grief:

King of dharma, why do you approve of unrighteousness, concerning this fallen man whose kinsmen are slain and whose wits are gone?
mahabharata:9:59.30	Why, though you know dharma, lord of men, do you look on while Bhima crushes Duryodhana's head with his foot?
[Yudhishthira said:] "This is not pleasing to me, Krishna, that Vrikodara touched the king's head with his foot in anger; nor do I rejoice in the ruin of the family.
We were ever cheated by deceit by the sons of Dhritarashtra, and sent to the forest after many harsh words.
'That sorrow of Bhimasena lies very deep in his heart'—thinking this, Vrishni, I overlooked it.
So, having slain the one of unwise mind, greedy and subject to desire, let the Pandava have his wish, whether in dharma or even in unrighteousness done."
[Sanjaya said:] When the king of dharma had said this, Vasudeva, hardly, the delight of the Yadu line, said, "Let it be so."
Thus addressed by Vasudeva, well-wisher of Bhima, he approved all that Bhima had done in the fight.
Bhimasena too, intolerant, having slain your son in the battle, stood before him, bowed, glad, with joined palms,
and said to the king of dharma Yudhishthira, greatly radiant, his eyes wide with joy, victorious, lord of men:

Today the earth is yours, O king, tranquil, her thorns slain; rule her, great king, keeping your own dharma.
mahabharata:9:59.40	He who was the doer of this enmity, fond of deceit by deceit, lies slain on the earth, lord of the earth.
mahabharata:9:59.41	Duhshasana and all those who spoke fiercely, Radheya (Karna) and Shakuni are slain, your foes.
mahabharata:9:59.42	This earth, filled with jewels, with her forests and mountains, has come back to you today, great king, your enemies slain.
[Yudhishthira said:] "The enmity has ended, King Suyodhana is slain, and by following Krishna's counsel this earth is won.
By good fortune you are free of the debt to your mother and to anger; by good fortune you have conquered the invincible; by good fortune the enemy is felled."
[Sanjaya said:] Having seen Duryodhana slain by Bhimasena in the battle, like a rutting forest elephant by a lion, great king,
the Pandavas with Krishna, the Panchalas and the Srinjayas there rejoiced when the delight of the Kurus was slain.
They waved their upper garments and gave lion-roars; the earth could not bear them, filled with such joy.
Some twanged bows, some twanged bowstrings, some blew great conches and others beat drums.
Others played, and your foes laughed, and the heroes repeatedly said to Bhimasena these words:

A hard deed, very great, you have done in battle today, having slain the king of the Kauravas in the fight with the mace, a great labour.
mahabharata:9:60.8	As Indra slew Vritra in the great battle, so people thought this slaying of the enemy was done by you.
mahabharata:9:60.9	Moving in many paths and circles on every side, this hero Duryodhana—who else but Vrikodara could slay him?
mahabharata:9:60.10	You have reached the far shore of the enmity, very hard for others; no one else could accomplish such a thing.
mahabharata:9:60.11	Like a rutting elephant, hero, at the head of the battle, you have, by good fortune, crushed Duryodhana's head with your foot.
mahabharata:9:60.12	Like a lion with a buffalo, having made a marvellous fight, you have by good fortune drunk Duhshasana's blood, blameless one.
mahabharata:9:60.13	Those who wronged the king, the righteous Yudhishthira, have had your foot placed on their heads, by good fortune, by your own deed.
mahabharata:9:60.14	By the slaying of Duryodhana and the overthrow of the enemies' seat, Bhima, by good fortune your great fame has spread on earth.
mahabharata:9:60.15	As bards delight in Shakra when Vritra was slain, so we delight in you, Bharata, with your enemies slain.
Know, Bharata, that the hairs that bristled at Duryodhana's slaying have not yet settled even today, said the weather-seers gathered there to Bhimasena.
To those delighted tigers among men, the Panchalas with the Pandavas, speaking thus, Madhusudana said what was fitting.

It is not right, lords of men, to slay a slain enemy again; this dull-witted one was already slain by fierce words repeatedly.
mahabharata:9:60.19	He was slain when, the sinful, shameless, greedy one, aided by sinners, transgressed his friends' counsel.
mahabharata:9:60.20	Though many times urged by Vidura, Drona, Kripa, the son of Ganga and the Srinjayas, he did not give the Pandavas their paternal share.
mahabharata:9:60.21	This vilest of men is today neither fit as friend nor as foe; what use to goad this one, like a log, with words?
mahabharata:9:60.22	Mount your chariots quickly, lords of the earth, let us go; by good fortune this sinful one is slain with his ministers, kinsmen and relatives.
Hearing this reproach from Krishna, King Duryodhana, falling under the sway of anger, rose, lord of men.
Sitting on his buttocks, propping up the earth with both arms, knitting his brows, he cast his glance at Vasudeva.
The king, with his body half raised, looked like an enraged venomous snake with its tail cut off, Bharata.
Heeding not the dreadful pain that would end his life, Duryodhana assailed Vasudeva with fierce words.

Son of Kamsa's slave! Are you not ashamed that I was felled by this unrighteous act in the mace-fight?
mahabharata:9:60.28	You falsely reminded Bhima, 'Break his thighs'; do I not know what you said to Arjuna?
mahabharata:9:60.29	Having had thousands of kings who fought straight slain by many crooked means, you have no shame, no disgust.
mahabharata:9:60.30	Day after day making great slaughter of heroes, you had your grandsire struck down by putting Shikhandin in front.
mahabharata:9:60.31	Having killed an elephant of Ashvatthaman's name, ill-minded one, you made the teacher lay down his weapon—do I not know that?
mahabharata:9:60.32	And that valiant one was seen felled by this cruel Dhrishtadyumna, and you did not prevent it.
mahabharata:9:60.33	Who is a greater sinner than you, who made Ghatotkacha waste the spear that was begged for the slaying of the son of Pandu?
mahabharata:9:60.34	The mighty Bhurishravas, with his arm cut off, sitting fasting, was slain by the evil-souled Shaineya, set on by you.
mahabharata:9:60.35	When Karna, doing his utmost to conquer Partha, was in difficulty with the serpent Ashvasena, son of the serpent king,
mahabharata:9:60.36	and again, when his wheel sank, afflicted by misfortune, defeated, Karna, leader of men, busied with his wheel, was felled in the battle.
mahabharata:9:60.37	If you had fought me, Karna, Bhishma and Drona fairly in the battle, your victory would surely not have been.
But by you, ignoble one, by crooked paths, kings who followed their own dharma were slain, and we and others.
[Vasudeva said:] "You are slain, son of Gandhari, with your brothers, sons and kinsmen, with your hosts and friends, having followed the path of sin.
By your own misdeeds the heroes Bhishma and Drona were felled, and Karna, who followed your ways, was slain in the battle.
Begged by me, fool, you would not give the Pandavas their paternal share, half the kingdom, from greed and by Shakuni's counsel.
You gave poison to Bhimasena, and ill-minded, burned all the Pandavas with their mother in the house of lac.
And Yajnaseni was dragged into the assembly at the dice-game in her season; even then, wicked one, you were to be slain, shameless one.
Because you, the dice-ignorant, were by the dice-knowing son of Subala cheated of a dharma-knowing one, therefore you are slain in battle.
Because sinful Jayadratha tormented Krishna in the forest when the Pandavas had gone hunting, at Trinabindu's hermitage,
and because Abhimanyu, a boy, alone, was slain in the battle by many through your faults, sinner, therefore you are slain in battle."
[Duryodhana said:] "I studied duly, I gave, I ruled the earth with her oceans, I stood on the heads of my foes—who is more fortunate than I?
What is desired by kshatriyas who look to their own dharma, this death I have obtained—who is more fortunate than I?
Human enjoyments fit for gods, hard for kings to attain, I have obtained; supreme lordship I have gained—who is more fortunate than I?
I shall go to heaven with my friends and kinsmen, Achyuta; you, your plans frustrated, will live on grieving."
[Sanjaya said:] At the close of these words of the king of the Kurus, Bharata, a great rain of holy-scented flowers fell.
Gandharvas played, hosts of Apsarases sang, and the perfected uttered cries of "Well done, well done," Bharata.
A fragrant wind blew, holy-scented, gentle and pleasant, and the sky shone spotless, like lapis lazuli.
Seeing those very wondrous things, those led by Vasudeva, seeing the honour paid to Duryodhana, became ashamed.
Hearing that they had been slain unrighteously, afflicted with grief, they sorrowed for Bhishma, Drona, Karna and Bhurishravas.
Seeing the Pandavas absorbed in thought, with dejected minds, Krishna, with a voice like a cloud-drum, said these words:

He and those great chariot-warriors, quick in weapons, valiant in fair fight, could not have been slain by you in the battle.
mahabharata:9:60.58	These means, lords of men, were devised by me; otherwise the Pandavas would never have had victory.
mahabharata:9:60.59	For those four great souls, mighty on earth, could not be slain by dharma even by the guardians of the world themselves.
mahabharata:9:60.60	Likewise this son of Dhritarashtra, mace in hand and unwearied, could not be slain by dharma even by Time, the wielder of the rod.
mahabharata:9:60.61	And do not take to heart that this king was slain; many foes, stronger, must be slain falsely by such means.
mahabharata:9:60.62	The path followed by the gods, slayers of the asuras, of old, and the road followed by the good—that is followed by all.
mahabharata:9:60.63	Our work is done; at evening we choose a resting place; with horses, elephants and chariots, lords of men, let us all rest.
Hearing Vasudeva's words, the Panchalas and Pandavas, greatly delighted, roared together like a band.
Then Madhava blew the Panchajanya conch, and the bulls among men, glad, saw Duryodhana slain.

And as the Pandavas went to the camp, Yuyutsu, the great archer, followed behind, lord of men, and Satyaki too.
mahabharata:9:61.3	Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin and all the sons of Draupadi, and all the other great archers, went to their own camps.
mahabharata:9:61.4	Then the Parthas entered Duryodhana's camp, its splendour gone and its lord slain, like a stage with the people dispersed.
mahabharata:9:61.5	Like a city where the festival has ended, like a lake whose elephants are taken, filled mostly with eunuchs and women, guarded by aged ministers,
mahabharata:9:61.6	there those led by Duryodhana's attendants waited on them, O king, with joined palms, clad in soiled ochre garments.
mahabharata:9:61.7	Reaching the camp of the king of the Kurus, the Pandavas, best of chariot-warriors, descended from their chariots, great king.
mahabharata:9:61.8	Then Keshava, ever intent on their good, said to the wielder of the Gandiva bow, bull of the Bharatas:
mahabharata:9:61.9	Lay down the Gandiva and the two inexhaustible great quivers; afterwards I shall descend, best of the Bharatas.
You yourself descend first; this is better for you, blameless one." And the hero, the son of Pandu, Dhananjaya, did so.
Then, afterwards, wise Krishna, letting go the reins of the horses, descended from the chariot of the wielder of Gandiva.
As soon as the great-souled lord of beings had descended, the divine ape-banner of the wielder of Gandiva vanished.
That great chariot, burned by the divine weapons of Drona and Karna, then blazed with fire at once, O king.
With its trappings and reins, its horses and yoke and fastenings, it fell to the ground, turned to ashes, the chariot of the wielder of Gandiva.
This bird has given me a teaching in the battle: that it is fitting to destroy enemies, and I think the time has come.
They came from invisibility and went again into invisibility; they are not yours nor you theirs—what is there to lament in that?
I wish to hear all from you, revered one, as it truly is; for you know all and are learned, and know in the world what is done and undone.
[Bhishma said:] While the serpent spoke thus, urged by Death, Death himself came and said this to the serpent:
By sacrifice, austerity and giving, O king, tiger among kings, men who do evil deeds are purified.
Having Brahmanas recite blessings and offering oblations to the fire, that king prayed for long life for the sons of Pandu.
The fourteenth and fifteenth of the dark fortnight have been made one again by Rahu; and so it was in the Bharata war, and has now come for our destruction.
Passing beyond that, they saw an ocean of sand, and looked upon the great mountain Meru, best of mountains.
Pursued by iron-beaked crows, ravens and vultures, and surrounded by needle-mouthed ghosts as huge as Vindhya mountains.
